title: Rivers to the sea
hookLine: the Tao in the world is like rivers flowing to the sea (Tao Te Ching 32)

lines: RAIN DOESN'T DECIDE WHERE TO GO.
WHERE ALL THE WATER ENDS UP.
cards: Rain hitting a roof doesn't decide where to go. It runs to the gutter, the gutter to the drain, the drain to a creek, the creek to a river. Nobody steers it.

Nobody has to persuade a single drop. After two days of armies and weapons, chapter thirty-two of the Tao Te Ching turns to something much quieter: water going downhill, and dew settling on the ground.
Its last line describes the Tao by the place where all the water ends up.

teach.h: SMALL, AND NOBODY CAN MASTER IT.
teach.b: First, the small thing nobody can master. The chapter opens by saying the Tao has no name. In its plain simplicity it may look small, and yet nobody in the world can make it a servant.

Small is not the same as weak. Second, the dew. Heaven and earth come together, the chapter says, and send down sweet dew, and the dew reaches everywhere evenly, of its own accord, without anyone giving orders.
No official decides which field gets watered.

teach.h: THE DEW FALLS ON EVERY FIELD.
teach.b: It just falls, and it falls on all of them. Third, names and stopping.

teach.h: NAMES, AND KNOWING WHERE TO STOP.
teach.b: Once things are shaped and divided, they get names, and once there are names, it's time to know where to stop. Legge's wording is that people can then know to rest in it, and so stay clear of failure.
Some readers hear a warning in that: naming is useful, but endless sorting and labeling is where things go wrong. Fourth, the sea.

The chapter closes, in James Legge's translation: "The relation of the Tao to all the world is like that of the great rivers and seas to the streams from the valleys." The streams aren't dragged to the sea.
They arrive because the sea is low and open, and water goes where it's received.
It can be a picture of a person, too: the kitchen everyone drifts into at a party, the friend people call first. Not because they grabbed. Because there's room.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter thirty-two as a picture of influence without force: like the sea that streams flow into, the Tao draws things by being low and open rather than by pulling.

games.q: what does “rivers to the sea” mean?
o: the Tao: the low, open place everything flows to
the Tao: a force that drags all things down
the Tao: a wall that keeps the rivers apart

p: nameless, small, and no one's servant
falls evenly, of its own accord
a sign it's time to know where to stop
flow into the great rivers and seas

s: chapter thirty-two says the Tao is small, so it's easy to master
it says though it may look small in its simplicity, nobody in the world can make it a servant.
the chapter says the sweet dew falls evenly without anyone directing it
heaven and earth send it down, and it reaches everywhere of its own accord.
the chapter compares the Tao to the streams in the valleys
it compares the Tao to the great rivers and seas that those streams flow into.

games.q: you want the streams in the valleys to come to you. what does chapter thirty-two suggest?
o: dig channels and pull them in.
climb higher so they can see you.
be low and open, like the sea.
games.why: the chapter compares the Tao to the great rivers and seas: the streams arrive on their own, because water goes to the low place.

practice: Find some water, at a window, a sink, a glass, or in your memory: a creek, a gutter in the rain. Watch it move; it never argues with the slope, it just takes the next low place, without hurrying and without stopping.
Let your breath move at the same easy pace.

wordCard.voice: Rivers to the sea. Chapter thirty-two's closing picture: the Tao is to the world as the great rivers and seas are to the streams that run into them from the valleys. Today's word.
